session_title: Curatorial Theme and Preliminary Selection Dilemma
theme: 购物-为专题策展挑选物件

content.text: Gu Yanci, I've been working on the spring feature lately, with the theme 'Traces of Revival'. These are some photos of objects I've collected as a starting point, and I'd like to hear your thoughts.
For example, this repaired ceramic bowl, I think it has a strong sense of story.
Angelica, you're here again. Last time during the restaurant inspection, you kept getting carried away by the 'stories' and forgot about the visuals themselves. Let me take a look at these photos.
This ceramic bowl clearly shows the traces of kintsugi repair, but the lighting is too flat, failing to highlight the texture at all. Couldn't you adjust the angle before taking the photo?
I admit, I might be too focused on the meaning behind objects. Like that restaurant last time, I always try to find a narrative in the details.
This linen shirt has a faded and washed-out look, which I think reflects the wear and tear of everyday use.
Stop. Don't rush to tell the story. These objects—the clay bowl, the shirt, and the old rattan chair and notebook you mentioned earlier—they all share one thing in common: time.
But how is 'time' visually represented? Is it a smooth patina, or sharp cracks? Is it even fading, or localized stains? The visual language of what you've chosen now is chaotic and disorganized.
You're right. I seem to have fallen back into my old habit of only seeing the emotional aspect of 'traces' without systematically considering its visual grammar.
This notebook is quite worn at the edges, but I feel its fading is different from that of a shirt.

Finally, there's a bit of progress. The wear on the notebook is localized and irregular, while the fading of the shirt is more uniform. That's the visual difference. But your photos still have the same old issues—cluttered backgrounds and unfocused lighting.

When we were writing restaurant reviews, I emphasized visual order. The same applies now: you need to first define the visual core characteristics of "traces," otherwise these objects will just clash with each other when placed together.
I see. Just like last time when you criticized the menu layout, we can't rely solely on intuition; we need standards. Could you help me establish a visual standard for screening?

Yes. After all, we've collaborated a few times. Your narrative instinct, though annoying, can at least drive things forward. First, categorize the "traces": physical (such as cracks, wear) vs. chemical (such as fading, stains).
This classification is very useful! So, the kintsugi of the ceramic bowl is a physical repair, and the fading of the shirt is a chemical change?

Yes. But don't go off and start fabricating stories again. The focus is on the visual presentation: Are the lines of the kintsugi smooth? Is the gradient of the fading natural? We need consistent lighting and composition to evaluate.

I see. Just like when you analyzed the restaurant utensils earlier, both the tactile feel and visual aspects need to be considered. So, I'll reshoot these objects, focusing on the visual characteristics of 'traces,' and then have you review them?
Hmm. This time, don't send those flat-lit photos. Remember, visual grammar needs to be systematic—we've been emphasizing this from the last on-site inspection to the article collaboration.
Thank you! Your sharp tongue is still as direct as ever, but it really helped me clarify my thoughts. Let's stay in touch, and I'll send you the new photos once I've taken them.
Okay. But hurry up, don't drag your feet like last time with the restaurant feedback. Once the visual standards are set, the subsequent screening can be efficient.
